# Elasticsearch 

 📅 Last updated on 07 October 2026 🤖 

Elasticsearch is a search engine that provides a distributed, multi-tenant-capable full-text search engine with an HTTP web interface and schema-free JSON documents.

| Show more unmaintained releases | | | |

Elasticsearch is part of the Elastic Stack, also known as the ELK Stack. It shares the same support policy as the other products in the Elastic Stack (Kibana, Logstash, Beats…).

Elastic Stack product releases follow Semantic Versioning. Elastic provides maintenance for each major release series for the longest of 30 months after the GA date of the major release or 18 months after the GA date of the following major release. For example, if version 1.0 was released on 10-Apr-2019 and version 2.0 was released on 10-Feb-2022.

- 30 months from 1.0 GA date is 10-Oct-2021
- 18 months from 2.0 GA date is 10-Aug-2023
- 1.x maintenance would end on 10-Aug-2023

End-of-life dates for Elasticsearch can be found on the Elastic product EOL dates page. Support for various operating systems can also be found on the Elastic support matrix page. License information can be found on the Elastic license page.

More information is available on the Elasticsearch website.

You should be running one of the supported release numbers listed above in the rightmost column.

> ```
> $ES_HOME/bin/elasticsearch -v
> ```

results.title: Elasticsearch Metrics: 1,284 Commits, 17 Releases, and the Open-Core Tradeoff | ToolVitals
results.author: ToolVitals Research
results.text:
Elasticsearch Metrics: 1,284 Commits, 17 Releases, and the Open-Core Tradeoff | ToolVitals

October 13, 2026 Databases by ToolVitals Research

# Elasticsearch Metrics: 1,284 Commits, 17 Releases, and the Open-Core Tradeoff

Elasticsearch is not showing a simple healthy-project story: ToolVitals records 1,284 GitHub commits in the last 30 days, 99 active contributors, a 98 health score, and a 98 shipping score. Yet the same payload reports 0 release events in 30 days, alongside 17 GitHub releases in 90 days. The gap is the real signal: development is busy, but the public release surface does not line up cleanly with that activity. Elasticsearch deserves evaluation as an active platform with a complicated delivery model, not as a star count with a database attached.

## Elasticsearch is broader than a search box

Elastic’s official Elasticsearch page positions the product as a distributed search, analytics, and AI platform. The page says Elasticsearch stores structured, unstructured, and vector data in real time, then supports full-text, hybrid, and vector search. It also presents observability and security analytics as central uses, not as unrelated add-ons.

The GitHub repository gives the same product a more engineering-focused description. It calls Elasticsearch a distributed search and analytics engine, a scalable data store, and a vector database optimized for speed and relevance on production-scale workloads. The repository also names retrieval-augmented generation and application performance monitoring as use cases.

That positioning changes the problem Elasticsearch is trying to solve. This is not only a document index for a search box. It is intended to keep multiple data types available for retrieval, analytics, monitoring, and AI-backed applications through a common system and API surface.

The benefit is architectural consolidation. A team can investigate one platform for text search, structured data, vectors, operational signals, and security data instead of assembling a separate product for each workload. The cost is evaluation complexity. A system that claims to serve several workload classes must be tested against each one, because a strong result in text search does not prove an equally strong result for vector retrieval, high-cardinality analytics, or operational monitoring.

## The metrics show activity, not a finished verdict

ToolVitals gives Elasticsearch a hot score of 216.7 and a ToolVitals score of 98. The repository has 78,227 GitHub stars, 1,284 commits in the 30-day window, 99 active contributors, and 17 GitHub releases in the 90-day window. Its health score is 98, its shipping score is 98, its 30-day release-event count is 0, and the payload assigns the data a confidence score of 90.

Those numbers support a clear claim about public project activity. Elasticsearch is not a dormant repository, and its development is spread across a large active contributor set. The high health and shipping scores also show that ToolVitals sees the project as well maintained and active according to its own measurements.

They do not support every conclusion a buyer might want. GitHub stars are accumulated attention, not a current usage count. A commit can represent a feature, a test, a refactor, documentation, a backport, or a merge. The active-contributor figure does not show how work is distributed across maintainers, vendors, or occasional contributors.

The release numbers need the same careful reading. ToolVitals reports 17 GitHub releases over 90 days but 0 release events over 30 days. The recent event data includes an Elasticsearch 9.5.2 GitHub release dated August 20, 2026, so the fields are clearly describing different windows or event definitions rather than one unified release counter. The safe interpretation is that Elasticsearch has substantial recent release history, while the current 30-day event metric does not show a release event.

## Descriptions

(2)

Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (CWE-400) in Elasticsearch can lead to denial of service via Excessive Allocation (CAPEC-130). A low-privileged authenticated user can submit a specially crafted query that causes uncontrolled memory growth in the query processing engine, resulting in an out-of-memory condition that terminates the Elasticsearch node. The condition can be triggered repeatedly, including by queries embedded in shared resources, causing persistent cluster unavailability.

A flaw was found in Elasticsearch. An authenticated remote attacker with low privileges can submit a specially crafted query to the query processing engine, triggering excessive memory allocation. This uncontrolled memory growth leads to an out-of-memory crash that terminates the service node, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS) and cluster unavailability.
